opus-5.5.text:
Well, Picbreeder is a really interesting case because it was never designed to be a scientific instrument for studying creativity. It was just a website where people could breed images. You'd see a set of pictures, pick the ones you liked, and the system would generate offspring. Other people could then branch off from what you'd found. Over time you got this big phylogeny of images, thousands of lineages, and some of them ended up looking like real things: a skull, a car, a butterfly, a face.

What struck me, and what I think tells us something about deep insight, is how those images were actually discovered. When we traced the lineages back, the people who found the skull or the car almost never set out to find it. The steppingstones leading to the skull didn't look like skulls at all. Someone was breeding something that looked like a pair of eyes, or just an interesting symmetric blob, and only later did it turn into a skull. If you'd been trying to get a skull from the start, you'd never have picked those ancestors, because they didn't resemble the goal.

That's the paradox at the heart of it. For really ambitious discoveries, the objective can be deceptive. The things that lead you to the destination often don't resemble it. So if you only follow what looks like progress toward your goal, you cut yourself off from the path that actually gets there. We tested this too: when we took those Picbreeder images as targets and tried to evolve them directly with a conventional objective-driven algorithm, it basically failed, even though humans had found them easily without trying.

So what does that say about creative insight? I think a lot of deep insights come from people following what's interesting rather than what's aligned with a fixed goal. You collect steppingstones because they're novel, because they open up new possibilities, and you can't always justify them in advance. Then, at some point, you recognize that you're one step away from something remarkable that you couldn't even have conceived of at the start. Insight in that view isn't a straight march; it's opportunistic. It's being in the right place in the search space and having the sensitivity to notice.

There's another aspect: it was collective. Picbreeder worked because many people with different tastes were branching off each other's work. No single person had a plan for the whole system. That's a lot like science and culture in general. Ideas get passed around, someone picks up a half-finished thing for their own reasons, and it turns into something nobody anticipated. If you imposed a single committee objective on all of it, you'd probably kill the very diversity that makes the breakthroughs possible.

And I think this matters for AI now. If we want machines that are genuinely creative, that keep producing new insights indefinitely rather than optimizing toward a benchmark, they need some notion of interestingness, some way to value steppingstones for their own sake. Picbreeder is a small window into what that kind of open-ended process looks like when humans are the ones doing the judging. The question is whether we can capture that judgment in a system and let it run.

r001.rationale: The response describes branching image lineages and steppingstones, but does not say search builds a representational hierarchy by elaborating established regularities.

r002.rationale: It notes that some images came to resemble real things, but does not describe representational dimensions incidentally aligning with real-world structure.

r003.rationale: It does not compare Picbreeder’s limited interaction with Move 37’s emergence through millions of game trials.

r004.rationale: It discusses unexpected discoveries and recognizing a promising path, but does not propose that insight arises from accumulated representational hierarchy serendipitously aligning with reality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, Picbreeder is this thing we built a long time ago now, back in the late 2000s, where people on the internet would evolve pictures. You see a grid of images, you pick the one you like, it has children, you pick again, and you can also branch off from pictures other people have published. And the thing that I think is really profound about it, and it took me a long time to appreciate how profound it was, is that nobody could set out to find anything in particular. If you went in there saying "I'm going to evolve a car," you'd fail. Almost every time. But cars got discovered. Skulls got discovered, butterflies, faces. And they got discovered by people who weren't looking for them.

The famous example for me is the car. That came from someone who was working on an alien face, and the eyes of the alien face sort of drifted down and became wheels. And the person just noticed it, said "oh, that looks like a car," and went with it. So the stepping stone to the car was not something that looked like a car at all. It was a face. And if you had been optimizing for "car-ness," you would have thrown the face away, because it scores terribly on car-ness.

I think that's basically how deep creative insight works in people, too. The precursors to a big insight usually don't resemble the insight. If you look at the history of science or art or technology, the stepping stones look nothing like the destination. Vacuum tubes weren't invented by people trying to build computers. They were working on electricity and electrical phenomena. So the search is open-ended, it's divergent, it's driven by interestingness and novelty rather than by progress toward a fixed objective. And the thing that makes it work is that you collect stepping stones, you keep the interesting stuff around, even when you have no idea what it's for.

The other piece that I think is really important, and this connects to the stuff we later wrote about, is what those discoveries look like underneath. When you look inside the networks that produced those Picbreeder images, the representations are shockingly clean. The symmetry of a face is captured by a single part of the network. You can take one weight and it opens and closes the mouth. Nobody optimized for that, and in fact when you try to get those same images by just optimizing directly for them with gradient descent, you get a complete mess inside, what we started calling a fractured, entangled representation. It matches the picture, but the representation is garbage.

So open-ended search isn't just finding things you couldn't have aimed at. It's finding them in a way that produces understanding, in a sense, a representation that reflects the real regularities of the thing. And I think that's a lot of what we mean by insight when a human has one. It's not just that you got to the answer, it's that something clicked into a form that's elegant and decomposable and you can build on it. The reason the search can do that is that at every step someone's holding something that's genuinely interesting in its own right, so the structure that accumulates is structure that's actually meaningful, rather than whatever hack happened to reduce the loss.

So to me Picbreeder is almost like a little laboratory for creativity. It makes visible something that's usually hidden inside people's heads, which is that insight comes from following what's interesting, keeping the stepping stones, and not knowing where you're going. And I'd argue that a lot of what we're doing right now in AI, which is extremely objective-driven, is in some ways fighting against that.

r001.rationale: The response says meaningful structure accumulates through keeping interesting stepping stones, but does not describe a representational hierarchy built by elaborating previously established regularities.

r002.rationale: It says the network representation captures real regularities, such as facial symmetry and mouth movement, despite nobody optimizing for them.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare Picbreeder’s limited interaction with Move 37’s millions of game trials.

r004.rationale: It links human insight to meaningful accumulated structure, but does not propose that insight comes from a serendipitous alignment between a representational hierarchy and reality.

astra-6.text:
I think the striking thing about Picbreeder is that people often discover things they weren’t trying to discover. You’re evolving images, choosing what looks interesting, and perhaps you notice something that resembles a face. You follow that for a while, but then a variation suggests a car, and suddenly you’re going somewhere you never anticipated.

The important point is that the intermediate images might not look like progress toward the final image. If you had started with that final image as your objective, you might have rejected precisely the stepping stones that made it possible. Something can be essential to a discovery without looking anything like the discovery.

That gives us a way to think about creative insight. We tend to describe creativity retrospectively, as though somebody saw a destination and worked out how to reach it. But another possibility is that they accumulated interesting ideas without knowing what those ideas would eventually enable. Then, at some point, they recognized a connection—a possibility that wasn’t visible before.

Picbreeder makes that process tangible because you can look back through the ancestry of a discovery. You can see how surprising the path was. It suggests that pursuing what’s interesting isn’t merely a distraction from serious discovery. Sometimes it’s how we acquire the stepping stones that a direct pursuit of the objective would never find.

r002.rationale: The face and car examples concern what images may resemble; the response does not say that dimensions of a representation incidentally align with real-world structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most revealing things about Picbreeder is that people often discover something interesting while trying to make something else—or while not trying to make anything in particular. They see an image, some feature catches their attention, and they decide to explore it. Then, several steps later, that feature becomes part of something they never could have anticipated.

That gives us a way to think about creative insight. We tend to tell the story backward: once we have the discovery, we reconstruct a path that makes it look as though everything was leading there. But going forward, the important stepping stones might not look anything like the eventual result. If you were judging every intermediate idea by how close it was to your final goal, you might discard precisely the idea you needed.

In Picbreeder, you can actually look at those sequences. The ancestry of an interesting image lets you ask: would someone searching explicitly for this endpoint have chosen these ancestors? And sometimes the surprising answer is that the ancestors don't seem promising at all when viewed through that objective.

So I wouldn't say this explains all of human creativity. But it makes a particular mechanism tangible: deep insights can arise from accumulating interesting possibilities whose significance isn't yet apparent. The insight is partly recognizing that something you've encountered opens a door you didn't know was there. Open-ended search gives those encounters room to happen.
